rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the full elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Keep the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed while reducing gradient steepness to test whether the early three-peak cluster separates. This also reveals whether the later pair at R 1.52 gains enough resolution to permit subsequent time optimization.

The shallower gradient improved the early cluster but incurred a time penalty without resolving it. Test higher temperature against injection 1 to seek a selectivity improvement while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

At 60 C only one pair remains below baseline resolution, and there is substantial time margin. Lengthen the gradient to test whether that pair reaches R 1.5 while keeping the last peak within 10 minutes.

The remaining critical pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so further lengthening is unlikely to help. Raise the starting organic fraction to shift early-cluster selectivity while retaining the favorable 60 C temperature and a short elution time.
Increasing phi0 improved the critical pair from R 1.14 to 1.32 without compromising the other pairs. Take one more grid step to seek full resolution and shorten elution further.

Injection 6 reached the maximum CRF, so now test a shorter gradient for equally complete resolution in less time. Keep the endpoints and temperature fixed to measure the resolution cost of shortening tG by one grid step.
The 8-minute gradient narrowly missed full resolution. Lowering phi1 to 0.85 modestly reduces its slope, targeting recovery of both critical pairs while keeping elution faster than injection 6.

Injection 8 preserves maximum CRF with faster elution than injection 6. Test one higher starting-organic step to shorten retention further, watching for loss of resolution in the early cluster or near-unretained first peaks.

Keep injection 8 as the fastest fully resolved method so far. Probe the opposite temperature extreme for a different elution order and potentially wider selectivity margins that could support a faster gradient.

Return to the successful high-temperature selectivity and test a slope between injections 7 and 8, using a tighter solvent window. This may retain full resolution while reducing the last-peak time below 6.04 minutes; phi1 0.70 remains above the previous last-peak elution fraction.

At phi0 0.20, the early cluster had only one deficient pair, while the neighboring pair gained resolution. Lengthen that gradient by one step to test whether both pairs can exceed R 1.5 with a stronger minimum-resolution margin.

Return to the starting fraction that achieved full resolution and modestly reduce the slope to build resolution margin. The last peak should remain comfortably below 10 minutes, so this tests a potentially more robust maximum-score method while retaining injection 8 as the faster option.

Shorten injection 17's programmed gradient while narrowing its window to preserve nearly the same slope. This should slightly reduce retention while testing whether its critical pair retains R at least 1.5.

Test the remaining endpoint step between fully resolved injection 8 and faster, under-resolved injection 7. This directly checks whether the fastest confirmed maximum-score method can be shortened without losing full pair credit.
